col-du-galibier.intro: In the Tour de France since 1911 and often its highest point. The summit road climbs above the old tunnel, and on the south side a monument honours the Tour's founder Henri Desgrange.

sides.character: From Valloire a long moderate run up an open high valley to Plan Lachat, then it steepens through the hairpins below the top. The hard side, best saved for the climb.
sides.highlights: The hairpins from Plan Lachat, at the top the view across to the Écrins.

sides.character: Short and even from the Col du Lautaret, open and treeless, with wide views into the Écrins. A flowing, readable descent.
sides.highlights: The Desgrange monument and La Meije opposite.

alpe-d-huez.intro: The 21 numbered hairpins, each named after stage winners, make this the Tour's best-known climb. Fausto Coppi won the first summit finish here in 1952; today the fans party at Dutch Corner.

sides.character: From Bourg d'Oisans straight into steep hairpins, after which the gradient keeps changing. The signs count the hairpins down to the ski resort.
sides.highlights: Dutch Corner at hairpin 7 and the view back over the Oisans.

col-de-l-iseran.intro: The highest road pass in the Alps links the Haute Maurienne with the Isère valley. In 2019 a Tour stage was stopped after the crossing because of hail and a mudslide.

sides.character: From Bonneval up a lonely, treeless high valley, with a changing gradient and hard pitches in the upper part. Wild and remote, the finer side to climb.
sides.highlights: The view back to Bonneval and the glaciers of the Haute Maurienne.

sides.character: From Val d'Isère gentle at first, then in hairpins through the ski area, steeper near the top. Wider and more even; a readable descent with Val d'Isère ahead.

l-ecot.intro: A short dead end from Bonneval-sur-Arc to the stone hamlet of L'Écot at the very head of the Haute Maurienne. A quiet extra at the end of an Iseran ride.

sides.character: Up the valley beside the young Arc without hairpins, steepening towards the hamlet. Little traffic, open meadows and glacier views.
sides.highlights: The old stone houses of L'Écot.

col-de-la-bonette.intro: The loop around the Cime de la Bonette is the highest paved road in France, and the Tour has crossed it several times. Two very long, lonely sides with military ruins from the old border defences.

sides.character: From Jausiers long and even through larches, then in many hairpins over the bare slopes at Restefond. A steady rhythm that suits the climb.
sides.highlights: The barracks at Restefond and finally the loop around the Cime.

sides.character: From Saint-Étienne-de-Tinée even longer, but even and with fewer hairpins, up a lonely valley with wide bends. A long, open descent.
sides.highlights: The ruins of the Camp des Fourches.

col-d-izoard.intro: The scree desert of the Casse Déserte makes the Izoard unmistakable; a memorial there honours Fausto Coppi and Louison Bobet. A Tour classic between Briançon and the Queyras.

sides.character: From Briançon via Cervières with flatter stretches, then many hairpins through larch forest to the top. Good climbing, a twisty descent.
sides.highlights: The memorial at the top with the view back to the Écrins.

sides.character: From Guillestre long and flat at first through the Guil gorge, steeper from Arvieux, finally through the Casse Déserte. The classic climb, with its highlight at the end.
sides.highlights: The Casse Déserte with the Coppi–Bobet memorial.

ceillac-vallee-du-melezet.intro: A quiet dead end from the Guil valley up to Ceillac and on into the Vallée du Mélézet. A peaceful counterpoint to the big passes of the Queyras.

sides.character: From the Maison du Roy straight into steep hairpins out of the valley, then flatter steps to Ceillac and a final rise into the valley head.
sides.highlights: The village of Ceillac in its wide basin.

haute-vallee-de-cervieres.intro: A gentle detour off the Izoard's north side into a remote high valley. Little traffic and wide pastures, more of a cruise than a climb.

sides.character: Up the valley from Cervières in steps, mostly flat, with a few short ramps and small dips. Open country without any rush.

col-de-la-madeleine.intro: A regular on the Tour since 1969, with two very long sides between the Maurienne and the Tarentaise. A pass for endurance, hardly spectacular but honestly hard.

sides.character: From La Chambre almost constantly around 8 %, many hairpins through forest and pasture, with no let-up. The steady rhythm rewards the climb.
sides.highlights: At the top a view as far as Mont Blanc.

sides.character: From the Isère side uneven: steep pitches, flat stretches and a short dip. As a descent it is varied, with breathers in between.

col-de-la-croix-de-fer.intro: Named after the iron cross at the top and often ridden together with the nearby Glandon. A long, restless pass with counter-climbs between the Maurienne and the Oisans.

sides.character: From Saint-Jean-de-Maurienne long and stepped, with flat stretches and counter-climbs, then via Saint-Sorlin-d'Arves through open pasture.
sides.highlights: The Aiguilles d'Arves above Saint-Sorlin.

sides.character: From the Oisans via Allemont, with a long intermediate descent that gives away much height, then past the Lac de Grand Maison. Up and down in either direction.
sides.highlights: The Grand Maison reservoir below the top.

col-de-la-loze.intro: Only on the Tour since 2020, and a legend at once: the upper part is a narrow, car-free cycle road with constantly changing ramps. In 2023 Tadej Pogačar cracked here, and Jonas Vingegaard turned his yellow jersey into a decisive lead.

sides.character: From Brides-les-Bains on the road to Méribel, then on the cycle road with short steep ramps and flat bits to the top. Made for climbing.
sides.highlights: The car-free cycle road above the treeline.

sides.character: From Courchevel shorter and calmer, through the ski area in hairpins to the top. The easier choice for the descent.

meribel-mottaret.intro: A gentle detour off the Loze climb through Méribel to the ski village of Mottaret. More a link than a climb.

sides.character: From Méribel up the valley in steps, mostly moderate, with short dips between the village parts. Ski-resort scenery rather than wilderness.

mont-ventoux.intro: The Giant of Provence stands alone above the plain, its bare limestone summit visible from far away. On the Tour since 1951; Tom Simpson died here in 1967. Three ascents, all with the wind as an opponent.

sides.character: From Bédoin gentle at first, then long and steep through the forest to Chalet Reynard, then across the scree towards the summit tower. The classic climb.
sides.highlights: The Tom Simpson memorial just below the summit.

sides.character: From Malaucène the steepest side, with hard pitches in the forest. As a descent wide and fast, with few hairpins.
sides.highlights: The view across to the Dentelles de Montmirail.

sides.character: From Sault the gentlest side, long and stepped through lavender fields and forest, joining the Bédoin road at Chalet Reynard for the summit.
sides.highlights: The lavender fields around Sault.

colle-dell-agnello.intro: The third-highest road pass in the Alps links the Varaita valley with the Queyras. In the 2016 Giro the race leader Steven Kruijswijk crashed into a snowbank on the descent here.

sides.character: From the Varaita valley very long and stepped, past the reservoir at Pontechianale, then steep and in hairpins above the treeline. The hard side, best ridden up.
sides.highlights: The Lago di Castello near Pontechianale.

sides.character: From Château-Ville-Vieille through the villages of the Queyras, steepening over wide pastures near the top. More even, and the better choice to descend.
sides.highlights: From the top a long view down into Italy.

saint-veran.intro: A short detour to one of the highest villages in Europe, with timber houses and sundials. Easy to combine with a ride over the Agnello.

sides.character: From the junction near Molines moderately steep over open slopes, a little steeper towards the village. Short and easy, with wide views over the Queyras.
sides.highlights: The timber houses of Saint-Véran.

colle-delle-finestre.intro: On the Giro since 2005 and one of Italy's hardest climbs: tarmac below, about eight kilometres of gravel above. In 2018 Chris Froome began his solo ride to overall victory here.

sides.character: From Susa through forest in countless hairpins, with no flat stretches, then on gravel above the treeline. Long, steadily steep, and no place for thin tyres in the wet.
sides.highlights: The gravel hairpins above the treeline.

passo-dello-stelvio.intro: The 48 numbered hairpins from Prad are the defining image of an Alpine pass. The second-highest road pass in the Alps is often the Giro's Cima Coppi, with the Ortler right opposite.

sides.character: From Prad moderate along the valley to Trafoi, then the wall of hairpins grows steeper to the top. You see what is coming, and it is best ridden up.
sides.highlights: The view down the hairpin wall and across to the Ortler.

sides.character: From Bormio even through galleries and hairpins, past the Umbrail junction. Wider bends, the better side for the descent.
sides.highlights: The baths of Bormio at the foot of the climb.

sulden.intro: A detour into the Sulden valley to the mountaineering village below the Ortler and the Königspitze. A fine addition to the Stelvio.

sides.character: From Gomagoi up the narrow valley, with a changing gradient and some hairpins; near the top the view opens onto the glaciers.
sides.highlights: The Ortler and the Königspitze at the head of the valley.

passo-di-gavia.intro: The snowstorm stage of the 1988 Giro, which put Andy Hampsten on course for overall victory, made the Gavia famous. Narrow, high and wild, with the Lago Bianco at the top.

sides.character: From Ponte di Legno narrow and ever steeper, with an unlit tunnel in the upper part. Superb going up, tricky going down.
sides.highlights: The Lago Bianco just before the top.

sides.character: From Bormio via Santa Caterina Valfurva, long and stepped with flatter sections, open pasture near the top. The more readable side for the descent.

rifugio-dei-forni.intro: A narrow dead end from Santa Caterina into the Valle dei Forni, up to the hut below the Forni glacier. Right in the Stelvio National Park.

sides.character: From Santa Caterina growing steeper through forest, with few hairpins, opening out at the top onto the glacier valley.
sides.highlights: The view of the Forni glacier.

passo-del-mortirolo.intro: On the Giro since 1990 and the byword for steepness; Marco Pantani's attack in 1994 made it a legend. No views, hardly any traffic, just forest and ramps.

sides.character: From Mazzo very steep from the start through forest and many hairpins, with no respite, a little easier only in the upper part. Only sensible as a climb.
sides.highlights: The Pantani memorial on the way up.

sides.character: From Monno much more moderate, with intermediate descents and short steep pitches. The side for the descent.

umbrailpass.intro: Switzerland's highest road pass, on the border just below the Stelvio. Part of it was still gravel until 2015; today it is paved throughout.

sides.character: From Santa Maria steadily steep in many hairpins through forest and then over open slopes. Quieter than the Stelvio, but hardly easier.
sides.highlights: At the top the road joins the Bormio side of the Stelvio.

furkapass.intro: James Bond filmed a car chase on the Furka for Goldfinger in 1964, and the empty Hotel Belvédère above the Rhône Glacier is still a photo stop. With the Grimsel and the Susten it makes a classic three-pass loop.

sides.character: From Realp steeper at first in hairpins, flatter near the top through an open, bare high valley. A readable descent.
From Gletsch up in hairpins, past the Hotel Belvédère, steeper near the top. Behind you lie the Grimsel hairpins.
sides.highlights: The Hotel Belvédère and the Rhône Glacier.

grimselpass.intro: Granite, reservoirs and the stack of hairpins above Gletsch define the Grimsel. Together with the Furka and the Susten it makes one of Switzerland's best-known pass loops.

sides.character: From Innertkirchen a long climb up the Haslital, with a changing gradient, through galleries and past the reservoirs in the granite landscape. A long, flowing descent.
sides.highlights: The Räterichsboden and Grimsel reservoirs.

sides.character: From Gletsch a short climb up a staircase of hairpins, flatter near the top. The hairpins lie in plain view ahead and are fun to climb.
sides.highlights: The Totensee at the top.

sustenpass.intro: Opened in 1946 and planned from the start for motor traffic. An even gradient, wide bends and the Steingletscher below the summit tunnel.

sides.character: From Innertkirchen very long up the Gadmental, in steps, then in hairpins past the Steingletscher near the top. The glacier comes into view as you climb.
sides.highlights: The Steingletscher and the Steinsee below the top.

sides.character: From Wassen even up the Meiental, hardly any hairpins, with tunnels and galleries. A flowing, readable descent.

nufenenpass.intro: The highest road pass lying entirely in Switzerland links the Goms with Ticino. Opened only in 1969, it is quieter than its neighbours the Furka and the Gotthard.

sides.character: From Ulrichen steadily steep up the Ägene valley, steeper still over bare slopes near the top. The hard side, better as a climb.
sides.highlights: The Gries reservoir with its wind turbines just before the top.

sides.character: From Airolo long and stepped up the Val Bedretto, flat at first, then in hairpins. A long, quiet descent.
sides.highlights: The quiet Val Bedretto.

gotthard-tremola.intro: The cobbled Tremola on the Ticino side is one of the finest hairpin roads in the Alps, built in the 19th century. Since the tunnel and the new road arrived, it belongs almost entirely to cyclists.

sides.character: From Airolo on the Tremola's cobbles, hairpin after hairpin at an even gradient up the gorge. A treat going up, bumpy going down.
sides.highlights: The Tremola's granite-paved hairpins.

sides.character: From Hospental on the modern road, even and with few hairpins up an open high valley. Wide and smooth, the side for the descent.

grosse-scheidegg.intro: Closed to cars, with only the PostBus running: the Grosse Scheidegg is a quiet mountain road between Meiringen and Grindelwald. At the top you stand right below the Wetterhorn and the Eiger.

sides.character: From Meiringen past the Reichenbach Falls up the Reichenbach valley via Rosenlaui and Schwarzwaldalp, irregular with steep pitches. Long, quiet and varied.
sides.highlights: The Reichenbach Falls near Meiringen.

sides.character: From Grindelwald steep over open pasture, steeper near the top. As a descent the Eiger and the Wetterhorn are ahead of you, but it is narrow with oncoming PostBuses.
sides.highlights: The Eiger north face opposite.

klausenpass.intro: Between 1922 and 1934 the Klausen hill climb for cars was held here. The pass links Uri with Glarus, with the wide Urnerboden on its eastern side.

sides.character: From Altdorf long up the Schächental, stepped with flatter sections and steeper pitches, open slopes near the top. A long, quick descent.
From Linthal steeply up in hairpins, then flat across the Urnerboden and finally in hairpins below rock walls to the top. Varied and good for climbing.
sides.highlights: The Urnerboden, Switzerland's largest alpine pasture.

albulapass.intro: A quiet pass between the Albula valley and the Engadine, for long stretches beside the Rhaetian Railway's Albula line with its viaducts and spiral tunnels. Little traffic, plenty of landscape.

sides.character: From Filisur via Bergün and Preda in steps, with a tight rock passage at the Bergünerstein, then across an open plateau to the top.
sides.highlights: The Lai da Palpuogna above Preda.

sides.character: From La Punt short and steep at first in hairpins, flatter near the top. A short descent with views into the Engadine.
sides.highlights: The view down into the Upper Engadine.

col-du-grand-saint-bernard.intro: Crossed since Roman times and by Napoleon's army in 1800; at the top stands the hospice, home of the St Bernard dogs. Since the tunnel took the traffic, the old pass road is quieter.

sides.character: From Bourg-Saint-Pierre first on the tunnel road through galleries, then on the old pass road growing steeper to the hospice.
sides.highlights: The hospice by the lake at the top.

sides.character: From Etroubles via Saint-Rhémy even up a side valley of the Aosta valley, then in hairpins near the top. A calm, flowing descent.

grossglockner-hochalpenstrasse.intro: Opened in 1935 and still Austria's best-known scenic road, with views of the country's highest mountain. A long high-mountain crossing with two detours, to the Edelweißspitze and the Kaiser-Franz-Josefs-Höhe.

sides.character: From Fusch very long and stepped, in hairpins via Hochmais to the Fuscher Törl and with a short dip before the Hochtor. Wide and well built, a long, quick descent.
sides.highlights: The turn-off to the Edelweißspitze at the Fuscher Törl.

sides.character: From Heiligenblut steeper, in hairpins over open slopes, with the Großglockner in view. The shorter, harder side for climbing.
sides.highlights: The pilgrimage church of Heiligenblut against the Glockner.

edelweissspitze.intro: A short, steep cobbled detour to the highest point of the Glockner road. At the top a wide panorama over the Hohe Tauern.

sides.character: From the Fuscher Törl steadily steep in tight cobbled hairpins up to the viewpoint. Short but demanding.
sides.highlights: A panorama of more than 30 three-thousand-metre peaks.

kaiser-franz-josefs-hoehe.intro: The Gletscherstraße ends at the visitor centre facing the Großglockner, high above the Pasterze, Austria's longest glacier. A detour busy with day-trippers, best early in the day.

sides.character: From the Guttal in steps with a short dip, moderately steep over pasture, then along the slope to the end of the road.
sides.highlights: The Großglockner and the Pasterze straight opposite.

timmelsjoch.intro: The high road between the Ötztal and the Passeier valley is the last and hardest climb of the Ötztaler Radmarathon. On the South Tyrol side a long, wild road with tunnels.

sides.character: From Sölden via Hochgurgl, stepped with a dip and flatter sections. Wide and well built, the more pleasant side to descend.
From St. Leonhard very long up the Passeier valley, stepped, then in hairpins and through tunnels below rock walls near the top. The Ötztaler side, the one to climb.
sides.highlights: The hairpins below the rock walls just before the top.

silvretta-hochalpenstrasse.intro: The toll road between the Montafon and the Paznaun reaches the Bielerhöhe and the Silvretta reservoir at the top. On the Vorarlberg side a dense run of hairpins climbs to the Vermunt reservoir.

sides.character: From Partenen steeply up many hairpins to the Vermunt reservoir, then flatter along the water, with a dip, to the Bielerhöhe. The hairpins make the climb.
sides.highlights: The Vermunt and Silvretta reservoirs.

sides.character: From Galtür gentle and stepped up an open high valley, with few hairpins. A wide, calm descent.

kitzbueheler-horn.intro: A steep dead end from Kitzbühel up the town's own mountain, a regular summit finish of the Tour of Austria. At the top a wide view over the Kitzbühel Alps to the Wilder Kaiser.

sides.character: From Kitzbühel in steps, very steep ramps between short breathers and many hairpins over pasture. Hard all the way.
sides.highlights: The view to the Wilder Kaiser.

rossfeld-panoramastrasse.intro: Germany's highest high road runs as a loop along the border with Austria. At the top a wide view over the Salzach valley and up to the Hoher Göll.

sides.character: From Berchtesgaden steep and stepped, with a short dip, then along the slope on the panoramic road at the top.
sides.highlights: The Hoher Göll and the view into the Salzach valley.

passo-pordoi.intro: One of the four Sellaronda passes and one of the most-raced climbs of the Giro d'Italia. At the top a memorial recalls Fausto Coppi, with the Marmolada opposite.

sides.character: Short and even: from Arabba a ladder of hairpins climbs the open meadows of the east flank, with the next bends always in view ahead.
sides.highlights: At the top the Marmolada and its glacier straight across.

sides.character: The longer west side climbs evenly from Canazei through forest, then in many hairpins below the walls of the Sella massif.
sides.highlights: The rock walls of the Sella massif right above the road.

passo-giau.intro: For many the most beautiful pass in the Dolomites, with Ra Gusela and the Nuvolau almost within reach at the top. The steep south side is part of the Maratona dles Dolomites, and in 2021 the Giau was the Giro's Cima Coppi.

sides.character: The hard side: steep and irregular through forest from Selva di Cadore, then in tight hairpins over alpine meadows to the top. One to climb rather than descend.
sides.highlights: Ra Gusela and the Nuvolau rise up ahead of your front wheel.

sides.character: Longer and milder from Cortina, in steps via Pocol with flatter stretches between. Wide views of the Tofane make it the nicer way down.
sides.highlights: The Tofane above the Cortina basin.

passo-fedaia.intro: At the top the road runs along a reservoir beneath the Marmolada glacier, the largest in the Dolomites. The east side, with its long straight from Malga Ciapela, is among the hardest ramps around; in 2022 the Giro was decided here.

sides.character: Easy for a long time from Caprile, then from Malga Ciapela it suddenly turns steep: an almost straight ramp with few hairpins up to the reservoir. A test uphill, hard braking downhill.
sides.highlights: The Marmolada appears at the end of the straight.

sides.character: The gentlest way up, from Canazei: moderate through forest, a little steeper towards the end, then flat along the lake shore. Flowing on the way down.
sides.highlights: At the top the reservoir below the Marmolada's north face.

passo-sella.intro: The Sella sits between Val di Fassa and Val Gardena right beneath the Sella towers, with the Sassolungo next door. As part of the Sellaronda it is busy in summer.

sides.character: From Canazei on the Pordoi road at first, then the road branches off and climbs in steps, with a short drop on the way, in hairpins below the Sella towers.
sides.highlights: The Sella towers right above the last hairpins.

sides.character: Calmer from Wolkenstein, with flatter stretches via Plan de Gralba and few hairpins. Downhill you roll into Val Gardena with the Sassolungo in view.
sides.highlights: The Sassolungo beside the road.

tre-cime-di-lavaredo.intro: The toll road ends at the Rifugio Auronzo below the south faces of the Tre Cime. The Giro has finished here several times; in 2013 Vincenzo Nibali won in a snowstorm.

sides.character: Gentle at first from Lake Misurina, with a short drop after the toll booth, then the steep final kilometres in a few hairpins up to the car park at the hut.
sides.highlights: Start at Lake Misurina, the Tre Cime right above you at the top.

monte-zoncolan.intro: Since 2003 the Giro has kept coming back to the Zoncolan, and the side from Ovaro counts among the steepest climbs in professional cycling. The scenery is humbler than the reputation: forest, then pastures and ski runs at the top.

sides.character: A wall: narrow and irregularly steep through forest from Ovaro, hardly a let-up, with short tunnels near the top. One to ride up only.
sides.highlights: At the top the arena of the Giro finishes.

sides.character: The milder side from Sutrio via the ski area, with flatter stretches and hairpins; it only gets really steep near the end. The better way down.

col-de-vars.intro: The Vars links the Ubaye with Guillestre and often shares a Tour de France stage with the Izoard or the Bonette. The north side runs through the ski resort of Vars, the south side is short and lonely.

sides.character: Long and stepped: from Guillestre through villages and the resort of Vars, with flatter stretches between the ramps. Downhill wide bends and open views.
sides.highlights: The Refuge Napoléon two kilometres below the top, good for a break.

sides.character: Short and open: from the Ubaye it steepens towards the top, over alpine pastures with little forest.

col-du-lautaret.intro: The national road between the Oisans and Briançon is above all the approach to the Galibier, which branches off at the top. From the west you ride below the glaciers of La Meije, and there is an alpine botanical garden at the pass.

sides.character: A long valley climb in steps through the Romanche gorge with tunnels and short descents, past the Chambon reservoir and through La Grave. Because of the tunnels and the traffic, better uphill.
sides.highlights: At La Grave, La Meije and its glaciers.

sides.character: Gentle from Briançon, with no hairpins, up the Serre Chevalier valley on a wide road. Fast and clear on the way down.

col-du-glandon.intro: The Glandon lies a stone's throw from the Col de la Croix de Fer; the roads part just below the top. The north side ends with the steepest ramps, the south side passes the Grand Maison reservoir.

sides.character: Long from La Chambre: in steps through forest and pastures, with breathers on the way, and right at the end the steep ramps just before the top.
The south side goes up and down: ramps, a clear drop on the way, then along the reservoir. Heading down you have to take the counter-climb, but it is open and wide.
sides.highlights: Along the Lac de Grand Maison.

col-de-joux-plane.intro: The classic last climb before the descent to Morzine in the Tour de France; in 2000 Lance Armstrong suffered his famous bonk here. At the top a small lake and a view of Mont Blanc.

sides.character: Steadily steep from Samoëns with no real let-up: first through forest and hairpins, then over open pastures at the top. Not a place for a bad day.
sides.highlights: Mont Blanc appears over the last kilometres.

col-de-la-colombiere.intro: A Tour classic between the Arve valley and the Aravis, right below the limestone walls of the Bargy range. The two sides differ: steepening from Scionzier, even from Le Grand-Bornand.

sides.character: From Scionzier moderate for a long time to Le Reposoir, then it steepens and the last kilometres climb below the rock walls. A climb that builds.
sides.highlights: The charterhouse of Le Reposoir on the way.

sides.character: Even from Le Grand-Bornand over alpine meadows and in hairpins, with open views. The more flowing side downhill.

cormet-de-roselend.intro: Between the Beaufortain and the Tarentaise the Cormet passes the turquoise Lac de Roselend and climbs into a wide, bare high valley. Quiet, varied and one of the finest roads in Savoy.

sides.character: Stepped from Beaufort: through forest to the Col du Méraillet, flat along the reservoir, then up once more into the high valley. The breaks make it a lovely way up.
sides.highlights: The Lac de Roselend with its chapel on the shore.

sides.character: Even from Bourg-Saint-Maurice in hairpins through forest and open ground. Easy to read and quick on the way down.

col-du-petit-saint-bernard.intro: The Romans already used this border pass between the Tarentaise and the Aosta Valley. At the top stand a statue of St Bernard and a prehistoric stone circle, with a view of Mont Blanc's south side.

sides.character: Long and irregular from Bourg-Saint-Maurice: in hairpins up to La Rosière, then more open and varying in gradient up to the border.
sides.highlights: At La Rosière the view back down the Tarentaise.

sides.character: Shorter and even from La Thuile, in regular hairpins over pastures. Rhythmic and easy to read on the way down.
sides.highlights: The Lac Verney just before the border.

col-du-mont-cenis.intro: Napoleon had the road over the Mont Cenis built up; at the top a wide plateau opens with a large reservoir. A short north side from the Maurienne faces a long south ramp from Susa.

sides.character: Short from Lanslebourg, with a few wide hairpins through forest, a little steeper towards the end. Quick and clear going down.
sides.highlights: At the top the plateau opens with the lake.

sides.character: The long south ramp climbs out of the Susa valley in steps and many hairpins past hamlets, before reaching the plateau and running along the reservoir to the pass.
sides.highlights: The last kilometres along the reservoir shore.

col-de-la-cayolle.intro: The Cayolle links Barcelonnette with the upper Var valley and is part of the Route des Grandes Alpes. Narrow and hardly used, through the Bachelard gorge in the north and past the source of the Var in the south.

sides.character: From Barcelonnette first squeezed through the Bachelard gorge, then in steps up an open high valley with flatter stretches. Gentle, long and lonely.
sides.highlights: The narrow Bachelard gorge in the lower part.

sides.character: Long and stepped from Guillaumes through the villages of the upper Var valley, never steep. Hardly any traffic either way.
sides.highlights: The Var rises near Estenc.

col-d-allos.intro: With the Cayolle and the Champs the Allos forms the triple loop from Barcelonnette. The north side is a narrow balcony road high above the Bachelard gorge, the south side climbs more calmly up the upper Verdon valley.

sides.character: Narrow and stepped from Barcelonnette along the flank above the gorge, often without a guard rail, then open pastures at the top. A joy uphill, delicate downhill.
Long and gentle from Colmars up the Verdon valley via Allos and La Foux, on a wider road. The better descent.
sides.highlights: The fortified old town of Colmars at the start.

col-des-champs.intro: The Champs is the quietest link between the Verdon and the Var: narrow, mediocre tarmac, wide pastures at the top. With the Allos and the Cayolle it forms the triple loop from Barcelonnette.

sides.character: Even from Colmars in hairpins through forest up to the pastures. Quiet, but the surface needs watching either way.
Longer from the Var valley with many hairpins, steepening towards the top. Because of the surface and the tight bends, better uphill.

col-de-la-lombarde.intro: From Isola the road climbs through the ski station of Isola 2000 to the Italian border, then winds down in many hairpins into the Stura valley to Vinadio. The Giro crossed it in 2016, finishing at Sant'Anna di Vinadio.

sides.character: Long and irregular out of the Tinée valley, with many hairpins up to Isola 2000 and above it on a wider road. The better descent of the two.
The Italian side is narrower: irregularly steep in many hairpins through forest and pastures, passing the turn-off to Sant'Anna near the top.
sides.highlights: The detour to the Santuario di Sant'Anna.

santuario-di-sant-anna-di-vinadio.intro: The sanctuary at just over 2000 m is said to be the highest in Europe and sits at the end of a short spur above the Lombarde road. A Giro stage finished here in 2016.

sides.character: A short, steadily steep spur up from the pass road, with only two hairpins up to the sanctuary.
sides.highlights: The pilgrimage church at the end of the road.

col-de-turini.intro: The Turini is famous from the night stages of the Monte Carlo Rally. Several roads meet at the top in the forest; from the east you come up the Bévéra valley from Sospel, from the west out of the Vésubie valley.

sides.character: Long and stepped: from Sospel through the narrow Piaon gorge, past Moulinet and then up through forest. Varied going down, but tight in the gorge.
sides.highlights: The Piaon gorge with the chapel of Notre-Dame-de-la-Menour.

sides.character: Shorter from La Bollène and steeper towards the top, with the stack of hairpins familiar from rally footage.
sides.highlights: The rally hairpins above La Bollène.

col-de-la-couillole.intro: A quiet crossing between the Tinée valley and Valberg that starts from very low down. Paris–Nice has finished at the top more than once; Tadej Pogačar won there in 2023.

sides.character: Long and even from Saint-Sauveur-sur-Tinée, in hairpins up bare slopes and past the perched village of Roubion. The real climb, narrow for a descent.
sides.highlights: The perched village of Roubion halfway up.

sides.character: Only a short step from Beuil, with a small dip on the way, over open upland. The easy way down.

colle-del-nivolet.intro: This dead end climbs through the Gran Paradiso National Park to over 2600 m, past the Serrù and Agnel reservoirs. In 2019 a Giro stage finished at Lago Serrù.

sides.character: Long and stepped: from Locana up the Orco valley with flatter stretches and tunnels to Ceresole Reale, then in many hairpins up to the lakes and the high valley.
sides.highlights: Lago Serrù and Lago Agnel below the last hairpins.

colle-fauniera.intro: Also called the Colle dei Morti: a narrow, high road between the Grana and Stura valleys, with the Pantani memorial at the top. The Granfondo Fausto Coppi from Cuneo crosses it.

sides.character: Long and even from Demonte up a lonely side valley, then over wide pastures. The surface is rough in either direction.
From the Grana valley it keeps steepening, the last kilometres being the hardest. Steep and rough, better up than down.
sides.highlights: The Santuario di San Magno in the upper Grana valley.

colle-di-sampeyre.intro: A high, narrow crossing between the Varaita and Maira valleys, steep from both sides and hardly used. From the top the view reaches the Monviso.

sides.character: The steeper side, from Sampeyre: irregular, with few hairpins, long through forest and then over pastures. Hard uphill, a long brake downhill.
Slightly milder from the Maira valley at Stroppo, with more hairpins and also irregular. The bends make the descent easier to read.

colle-san-carlo.intro: The short, hard crossing from Morgex to La Thuile averages almost ten per cent and sees little traffic. At the top the view opens onto Mont Blanc.

sides.character: A steadily steep wall out of the Aosta Valley: many hairpins through forest, no let-up. Only really a pleasure going up.
sides.highlights: The Mont Blanc view from the top.

sides.character: Short from La Thuile and also steadily steep, with few hairpins. The shorter way down.

simplonpass.intro: Napoleon had the Simplon road between Brig and Domodossola built; at the top stand the hospice and a stone eagle. Wide and busy, but even.

sides.character: Even from Brig on a wide road with few hairpins, across the Ganter bridge and through galleries.
sides.highlights: The Ganter bridge.

sides.character: From Gondo at the border through the narrow Gondo gorge with galleries, then more open past Simplon Dorf.
sides.highlights: The Gondo gorge.

lukmanierpass.intro: One of the gentlest Alpine crossings in Switzerland: from the Vorderrhein at Disentis into the Blenio valley in Ticino, past the Sontga Maria reservoir at the top. Little traffic, lots of space.

sides.character: From Disentis through the Medel gorge with tunnels, then in steps with a small dip up the wide Val Medel. Long and flowing on the way down.
sides.highlights: The gorge of the Medel Rhine beyond Disentis.

sides.character: Irregular from Olivone: steeper pieces in the lower part, then calmer up the upper Blenio valley to the top.
sides.highlights: The Sontga Maria reservoir at the top.

capanna-dotra.intro: A narrow spur off the Lukmanier's south side up to the Capanna Dötra on an alp above the Blenio valley. Hardly any traffic and a quiet detour.

sides.character: Steep and narrow straight from the junction, easing towards the top onto the alp.

oberalppass.intro: The Oberalp links Andermatt with the Surselva, with the railway carrying the Glacier Express beside the road. The lighthouse at the top recalls the nearby source of the Rhine in Lake Toma.

sides.character: From Andermatt first the wall of hairpins above the village, visible from below, then flatter across the upland to the top.
sides.highlights: The view back down to Andermatt from the hairpins.

sides.character: Long and stepped from Disentis through the Surselva villages via Sedrun, rarely steep. Wide and flowing on the way down.
sides.highlights: Disentis monastery at the start.

passo-san-bernardino.intro: Since the motorway tunnel took the traffic, the old pass road between the Misox and the Rheinwald has been quiet. At the top lies Lake Moesola among rocky knolls.

sides.character: Long and stepped from Mesocco, with a great many hairpins and flatter stretches via the village of San Bernardino. A climb with rhythm.
sides.highlights: The castle ruin of Mesocco at the start.

sides.character: Shorter and mild from Hinterrhein, stepped with a small dip on the way, the hairpins wide over open ground.
sides.highlights: Lake Moesola at the top.

spluegenpass.intro: The Splügen links the Rheinwald with Chiavenna. On the Swiss side the hairpins stack tightly one above the other; the Italian side climbs long from the valley, through galleries and past the Montespluga reservoir.

sides.character: Short and even from Splügen: a dense stairway of hairpins above the village, easy to read in either direction.
sides.highlights: The village of Splügen with its stone houses.

sides.character: Very long from Chiavenna, stepped with countless hairpins, some of them in galleries. Because of the tunnels and tight bends, better uphill.
sides.highlights: The Montespluga reservoir just before the border.

julierpass.intro: The Romans already crossed the Julier, and remains of a column still stand at the top. From the north a long climb up the Surses past the Marmorera reservoir, from Silvaplana short and direct.

sides.character: Long and stepped from Tiefencastel, with flatter stretches through the villages and along the reservoir, then hairpins over bare ground at the top.
sides.highlights: Along the Marmorera reservoir.

sides.character: Short from Silvaplana, steepest at the start and flatter higher up, with hardly a hairpin. On the way down the Engadin lakes lie ahead.
sides.highlights: The view over the Upper Engadin lakes.

malojapass.intro: The Maloja is only a pass on one side: from Chiavenna the Bregaglia climbs long, and at the top the road runs almost level into the Upper Engadin. The wall of hairpins right at the top is its trademark.

sides.character: Long and stepped up the Bregaglia via Castasegna and Vicosoprano with flatter stretches, finishing with the tight wall of hairpins below the top.
sides.highlights: Lake Sils just beyond the top.

berninapass.intro: The Bernina railway, a UNESCO World Heritage line, runs beside the road. From the north you look onto the Morteratsch glacier and Piz Palü; to the south the road drops steeply into the Italian-speaking Valposchiavo.

sides.character: Steadily and persistently steep from Poschiavo, through forest and then open via La Rösa, finally past Lago Bianco. The real climb.
sides.highlights: Lago Bianco just below the top.

sides.character: Gentle and stepped from Pontresina, almost without hairpins, with glaciers in view. Wide and flowing on the way down.
sides.highlights: The Morteratsch glacier and Piz Palü in view.

flueelapass.intro: The Flüela links Davos with the Lower Engadin; at the top there are two small mountain lakes and the hospice. The west side climbs calmly up a wide valley, the east side from Susch is steeper.

sides.character: Mild for a long time from Davos up an open high valley, a little steeper with a few hairpins at the top. Wide and clear on the way down.
Steadily steep from Susch in hairpins, first through forest, then over open slopes. The side for climbing.
sides.highlights: The hospice by the two lakes at the top.

ofenpass.intro: The Ofenpass crosses the Swiss National Park with its mountain pine forests and leads into the Val Müstair, home of St John's Abbey, a UNESCO World Heritage site.

sides.character: Long and without hairpins from Zernez through the National Park's forest, in steps with short descents along the way. A long, flowing run downhill.
sides.highlights: A break at the Hotel Il Fuorn in the middle of the park.

sides.character: Shorter and steeper from Santa Maria, stepped, with a few hairpins up the slopes of the Val Müstair.
sides.highlights: The abbey at Müstair a few kilometres from the start.

passo-del-foscagno.intro: Anyone heading from Bormio into duty-free Livigno has to cross the Foscagno; the customs post still stands at the top. From Livigno you first cross the Passo d'Eira, then drop briefly to Trepalle.

sides.character: Stepped from Isolaccia with flatter stretches and few hairpins up the Valdidentro, on a wide road.
From Livigno first over the Passo d'Eira, then briefly down to Trepalle and up again. Mild, but with a counter-climb in either direction.

passo-del-tonale.intro: The Tonale links the Valcamonica with the Val di Sole; at the top are a ski resort and the memorial to the fallen of the First World War, when the front ran through here. Often just the link to the Gavia or the Mortirolo.

sides.character: From Vezza d'Oglio gentle along the valley to Ponte di Legno at first, then steeper in hairpins up to the pass.
No hairpins from Vermiglio, steepest low down and flatter higher up, on a wide road. Fast downhill, but with traffic.

passo-san-marco.intro: The road follows the old Via Priula, which Venice had built from Bergamo to the Valtellina in the late 16th century. Today it is a quiet link between the Val Brembana and the Valtellina, and with some 1700 metres from Morbegno one of the longest climbs in the area.

sides.character: Out of the Valtellina through the Bitto valley: long and uneven, flatter stretches between steep ramps and a run of hairpins higher up. The big climb, better ridden uphill.
Out of the Val Brembana shorter, moderate low down, steeper higher up with hairpins over open slopes. As a descent the clearer choice.
sides.highlights: Ca' San Marco, the old inn on the Via Priula just below the top

passo-crocedomini.intro: A lonely high road in the Brescia Alps between the Val Camonica and the Val Caffaro. High pastures and hardly any cars at the top, but a surface that is coarse in many places.

sides.character: From Breno the hard side: around 8 % throughout, uneven, with many hairpins through forest up to the pastures. Steep and twisting, better uphill.
From Bagolino up the Val Caffaro, gentler on average, alternating between ramps and calmer stretches, with many hairpins. The milder descent.

oetztaler-gletscherstrasse.intro: Austria's highest tarmac road climbs from Sölden to the Rettenbach and Tiefenbach glaciers. Every autumn the Alpine Ski World Cup opens its season on the Rettenbach glacier. A climb almost entirely above the treeline, with little respite in the gradient.

sides.character: From Sölden past the toll booth and then long in double figures into the glacier valley, uneven with ramps. At the top nothing but rock, ice and ski lifts.
sides.highlights: Views back over the Ötztal and onto the glaciers of the Ötztal Alps

hochsoelden.intro: A short, steep detour off the glacier road up to the hotel hamlet of Hochsölden on a terrace high above the Ötztal. Only a few kilometres, but hardly ever below 10 %.

sides.character: Steep straight away from the junction, with a run of hairpins on the slope; it eases a little towards the end.
sides.highlights: View down onto Sölden and across to the peaks of the Ötztal Alps

kuehtai.intro: The crossing from the Ötztal into the Sellrain valley is the first climb of the Ötztaler Radmarathon, ridden from Ötz. At the top sits the ski village of Kühtai at just over 2000 m, reachable all year.

sides.character: From Kematen long and without hairpins up the Sellrain valley, a steady rise with a few steeper pitches higher up. As a descent long and flowing, as in the Ötztaler.
From Ötz the steeper side: uneven, ramps through forest and a few hairpins, more open higher up. The marathon direction and the better way up.

jaufenpass.intro: The Jaufen links the Passeier valley with Sterzing and is the third pass of the Ötztaler Radmarathon, ridden from Sterzing. Popular with motorcyclists; open pastures and views of the Texel group on the south side.

sides.character: From St. Leonhard steady and long, through forest and then in many hairpins over the sunny southern slopes. A rhythm that carries you uphill.
From Sterzing through the Jaufental, stepped with flatter stretches and few hairpins, mostly in forest. The Ötztaler direction; as a descent the faster side.

penserjoch.intro: The crossing from the Sarntal into the Wipptal near Sterzing is the quieter alternative to the Jaufen. Wide pastures above the treeline at the top, and from the south a long, easy run-in through the whole Sarntal.

sides.character: From Sarnthein long and stepped, with plenty of flat valley and the steeper part only at the top over the pastures. As a descent long and flowing.
From Sterzing much steeper, stepped with ramps and short breathers, through forest and then open pastures. The better way up.

hahntennjoch.intro: The Hahntennjoch links Imst with the Lech valley, its south side running through bare scree slopes. Popular with motorcyclists; since 2020 particularly loud machines have been banned.

sides.character: From the Lech valley via Bschlabs: up first, then some height is lost before the real climb leads in hairpins to the pass. Stepped and varied; as a descent it includes a climb back up.
From Imst the steep side, uneven with ramps, higher up through open scree slopes with a clear view back. A wall to ride uphill.
sides.highlights: View back into the Inn valley and onto the Lechtal Alps

arlbergpass.intro: The Arlberg divides Tyrol from Vorarlberg and is the watershed between the Rhine and the Danube. At the top stands St. Christoph with its hospice, which dates back to the 14th century. Despite the tunnel the pass road remains a busy route.

sides.character: From Pians long and flat up the Stanzertal to St. Anton; it only gets steeper in the final part to the top. Few hairpins, more a long valley ride than a pass.
From Langen via Stuben short and steeper, uneven with a series of hairpins below the Arlberg peaks. Compact, and uphill the more entertaining side.

gerlospass.intro: The Gerlos Alpine Road links the Zillertal with the upper Pinzgau, past the Durlassboden reservoir. On the Krimml side you look across to the Krimml Waterfalls, Austria's highest. A lot of traffic, but a gentle gradient.

sides.character: From Zell am Ziller first in hairpins out of the valley, then long and flatter through the Gerlos valley and along the reservoir. Stepped and long, the climb with a run-up.
From Krimml shorter, in wide hairpins above the Salzach valley with the waterfalls opposite. Descending, the view is ahead of you.
sides.highlights: View of the Krimml Waterfalls

malta-hochalmstrasse.intro: The toll road runs through the Malta valley, known for its waterfalls, up to the Kölnbrein dam, Austria's highest. On the way, waterfalls and narrow tunnels controlled by traffic lights.

sides.character: From Gmünd long and flat up the Malta valley, then stepped and steeper in hairpins and through tunnels up to the dam wall.
sides.highlights: The Kölnbrein dam and its reservoir in the Hohe Tauern

nockalmstrasse.intro: A panoramic road through the rounded summits of the Nock mountains in the biosphere park, with two high points: the Eisentalhöhe and the Schiestelscharte. More rollers than a pass, with many hairpins and wide pastures.

sides.character: From Innerkrems a short way to the Eisentalhöhe, stepped with flat stretches and a few hairpins over pastures.
From Ebene Reichenau the whole road: over the Schiestelscharte, a lot of height back down into the valley and up again to the Eisentalhöhe, with many hairpins. The side to ride uphill as a tour.

turracher-hoehe.intro: The crossing between Carinthia and Styria, with ramps of over 20 %, is considered one of Austria's steepest passes. At the top lies the Turracher See between ski lifts and Swiss stone pine forest.

sides.character: From Ebene Reichenau the classic side: alternating very steep ramps and flatter stretches, with hairpins. The steep bits are better ridden up.
From Predlitz through the Turrach valley, stepped with flat stretches between steeper sections and only a few hairpins.

soelkpass.intro: One of the few road crossings of the Niedere Tauern, through the Sölk valleys nature park from the Enns valley to the Mur valley. Little traffic, a lot of forest and a bare summit.

sides.character: From Stein an der Enns long through the Großsölk valley, stepped with flat stretches, steeper only higher up. As a descent long and quiet.
From Schöder shorter and steeper, the gradient increasing towards the top, with a few hairpins. The better way up.

villacher-alpenstrasse.intro: The toll road climbs from Villach onto the Dobratsch, the Villacher Alpe, in its nature park. Wide views at the top over the Carinthian lakes, the Karawanks and the Julian Alps.

sides.character: From the edge of town at a steady 6 to 7 % through forest, with a few hairpins and viewpoints, up to the Rosstratten car park.
sides.highlights: View from the Rosstratten onto the Julian Alps and the Karawanks

vrsic.intro: Slovenia's highest pass crosses the Julian Alps from Kranjska Gora to the Soča valley, with 50 numbered hairpins, cobbled on the north side. It was built in the First World War by Russian prisoners of war, remembered by the Russian Chapel.

sides.character: From Kranjska Gora past Lake Jasna, then through forest in cobbled hairpins, steeper towards the top. The cobbles speak against descending here.
sides.highlights: The Russian Chapel on the way, and Prisojnik and Mojstrovka at the top

sides.character: From the Trenta valley along the Soča and then in many hairpins up the southern flank, steeper towards the top. As a descent with views into the Soča valley.
sides.highlights: The emerald water of the Soča in the valley

mangart-sattel.intro: Slovenia's highest road was built as an Italian military road in the 1930s. With unlit tunnels and narrow ramps it climbs beneath the north faces of the Mangart, one of the wildest dead ends in the Eastern Alps.

sides.character: From Log pod Mangartom first towards the Predel, then onto the narrow mountain road: stepped, long stretches at 8 % and more, with hairpins, tunnels and ever wider views.
sides.highlights: The rock walls of the Mangart and the view across the Julian Alps

passo-falzarego.intro: The front line of the First World War ran between Cortina and Livinallongo; at the top the tunnels in the Lagazuoi recall it. The Falzarego is part of the Maratona dles Dolomites and a busy crossing all year round.

sides.character: From Cortina in wide hairpins through forest and then open ground below the Tofane and the Cinque Torri. Wide and clear; as a descent with views over the Ampezzo basin.
From Caprile long and stepped up into the Livinallongo, past Andraz castle and in many hairpins to the top. The longer side, better uphill.

cinque-torri.intro: A steep spur up to the five rock towers above Cortina, where Italian artillery stood in the First World War. Today the area is an open-air museum with restored positions.

sides.character: From the junction on the Falzarego road straight away at around 10 % and barely easing, with few hairpins, first through forest, then open below the towers.
sides.highlights: The five towers up close and views of the Tofana and the Croda da Lago

passo-valparola.intro: The Valparola lies only a little over a kilometre of road from the Falzarego and leads down into the Val Badia. At the top stands the Tre Sassi fort with a First World War museum, and a small lake below the Lagazuoi.

sides.character: From Stern via San Cassiano gently along the valley first, then stepped and steeper in hairpins over open pastures to the top.
sides.highlights: The Tre Sassi fort and the Valparola lake at the top

passo-gardena.intro: The Gardena pass links Val Gardena with the Val Badia and is one of the four Sellaronda passes. At the top the Sella towers rise on one side, the Cir peaks on the other.

sides.character: From Corvara via Colfosco at a steady 6 % in a run of hairpins below the Sassongher. A rhythm that carries you uphill.
From Wolkenstein stepped and gentler, with hairpins and short breathers, open at the top below the Cir peaks. As a descent with views of the Sella.

passo-campolongo.intro: The lowest and gentlest pass of the Sellaronda, between Corvara and Arabba. In the Maratona dles Dolomites it is the first climb.

sides.character: From Arabba short and steeper at first, with a few hairpins, flattening towards the top. A quick hop over the saddle.
From Corvara steady and moderate through meadows and forest, with a few hairpins. The Maratona direction; pleasant both up and down.

passo-rolle.intro: The Rolle passes beneath the Pale di San Martino, with the Cimon della Pala, the Matterhorn of the Dolomites, above the top. On the north side lies the Paneveggio forest, whose spruce violin makers prize as tonewood.

sides.character: From Predazzo long and stepped through the Paneveggio forest, with flatter stretches and hairpins only in the upper part. As a descent long and flowing.
From Fiera di Primiero via San Martino di Castrozza steady and long, with many hairpins and the Pale in front of you. The finer way up.
sides.highlights: The Pale di San Martino above San Martino di Castrozza

passo-san-pellegrino.intro: The San Pellegrino links the Fassa valley at Moena with the Biois valley and Falcade. At the top a broad saddle with a ski area; the east side is clearly the steeper one.

sides.character: From Moena steeper at first through forest, then easing, almost without hairpins to the broad top. As a descent straight and fast.
From Falcade steadily steep in a run of hairpins, with steeper ramps. The side for climbing.

passo-manghen.intro: The Manghen crosses the lonely Lagorai range between the Valsugana and the Fiemme valley. Narrow, steep and nearly free of traffic, and with over 1600 metres from the Valsugana one of the hardest climbs in Trentino.

sides.character: From Borgo Valsugana long and ever steeper towards the top, through forest and finally in hairpins over open slopes. The hard side, to be ridden uphill.
From Molina di Fiemme through the Val Cadino, stepped and more moderate, with a stretch that gives height back. The milder descent.

passo-delle-erbe.intro: The Würzjoch links the Val Badia with the Eisack valley near Brixen and lies right beneath the Peitlerkofel in the Puez-Odle nature park. Little traffic, narrow roads and alpine meadows.

sides.character: From St. Martin in Thurn stepped, with hairpins and a short downhill stretch, open at the top below the Peitlerkofel. As a descent the shorter side.
From Brixen long and stepped via the hillside villages, alternating between ramps and flatter stretches. The long climb, with the Peitlerkofel ahead as the goal.
sides.highlights: The Peitlerkofel right above the top

passo-staulanza.intro: The Staulanza links the Zoldo valley with Selva di Cadore and runs right along the west flank of the Pelmo. Quieter than the big Dolomite passes and open all year.

sides.character: From Forno di Zoldo long and stepped along the valley and then up in hairpins, briefly with a downhill stretch, the Pelmo in front of you.
sides.highlights: The Pelmo up close

sides.character: From Selva di Cadore short and moderate, with few hairpins through forest and meadows. As a descent short and clear.

passo-duran.intro: A quiet crossing between Agordo and the Zoldo valley, squeezed between the Moiazza and the San Sebastiano. Hardly any traffic, narrow, and with long, steep straights on the Agordo side.

sides.character: From Agordo steadily steep, almost without hairpins, through forest and past hamlets. Long steep straights, better ridden uphill.
From Forno di Zoldo stepped and more moderate, with a few hairpins and a short downhill stretch. The friendlier descent.

passo-monte-croce-comelico.intro: The Kreuzberg pass links the Sexten valley with the Comelico; in the First World War the front ran here. A gentle crossing with the Sexten Dolomites in view.

sides.character: From Innichen via Sexten flat and stepped, hardly any hairpins, the Sexten Dolomites in front of you. A calm roll both up and down.
sides.highlights: The Sexten Dolomites above the Fischleintal

sides.character: From Padola short, with ups and downs and a few hairpins through forest to the saddle.

combe-laval.intro: One of France's boldest roads: the final kilometres are blasted as a gallery into the sheer wall of the Cirque de Combe Laval. Over the Col de la Machine it climbs into the high valley of Lente in the Vercors.

sides.character: From Saint-Jean-en-Royans unevenly up through forest, then onto the ledge in the rock wall, with tunnels and the cirque below you.
sides.highlights: The view from the gallery down into the cirque and out over the Royans

gorges-de-la-bourne.intro: The road through the Bourne gorge is blasted into the rock wall for kilometres, single-track in places beneath overhanging rock. It links Pont-en-Royans with Villard-de-Lans and is one of the main approaches to the Vercors.

sides.character: From Pont-en-Royans upstream through the gorge, stepped and mostly gentle, with short steeper pitches, tunnels and rock overhangs, up onto the plateau at Villard-de-Lans.
sides.highlights: The houses hanging over the river at Pont-en-Royans, at the start

col-du-rousset.intro: The Rousset is the southern gateway to the Vercors: from Die the road winds up the dry southern flank, and its top is a tunnel. Beyond it the green high plateau opens up all at once.

sides.character: From Die long and gentle through the Diois, stepped with flatter sections, higher up in a run of hairpins below the cliffs to the tunnel.
sides.highlights: View from the hairpins down into the Drôme valley

col-du-granon.intro: A military road with no way through above Serre Chevalier, with nothing at the top but meadows and the Écrins opposite. Two Tour finishes made history: in 1986 Hinault lost the yellow jersey here, in 2022 Pogačar cracked against Vingegaard.

sides.character: From Saint-Chaffrey steep straight away and tougher still higher up, first through larches, then over open, shadeless pastures. Hardly a place to catch your breath.
sides.highlights: At the top the view of the Écrins and down into the Briançon valley

val-thorens.intro: The ascent to the highest ski resort in the Alps runs up the whole Belleville valley. In 2019 the last mountain stage of the Tour finished here, won by Vincenzo Nibali.

sides.character: From Moûtiers long and stepped via Saint-Martin-de-Belleville and Les Menuires, never steep, never flat, with many hairpins. Ski lifts rather than summit views at the top.

les-arcs.intro: The ski-resort ascent from Bourg-Saint-Maurice via Arc 1800 up to Arc 2000. In the 1996 Tour, Miguel Indurain cracked in the final kilometres to Les Arcs; his run of five Tour wins ended that year.

sides.character: From Bourg-Saint-Maurice stepped with many hairpins through forest and meadows, then up between the ski stations, with steeper ramps in between.
sides.highlights: View across the upper Tarentaise valley

orcieres-merlette.intro: A quiet ski resort in the Champsaur with a big Tour history: in 1971 Luis Ocaña rode away from Eddy Merckx here by almost nine minutes, and in 2020 Primož Roglič won the stage.

sides.character: From Pont-du-Fossé steady and moderate, stepped with hairpins above the Drac valley, up to the resort.

pra-loup.intro: This is where the Merckx era ended in 1975: Bernard Thévenet caught him on the climb to Pra-Loup and took the yellow jersey, which he wore to Paris. A short, even climb above Barcelonnette.

sides.character: From Barcelonnette even and moderate, stepped with a few hairpins through larch forest to the resort, with views back into the Ubaye valley.
sides.highlights: View across the Ubaye valley

le-chazelet.intro: A short dead end above La Grave that ends at the oratory, directly opposite the Meije and its glaciers. One of the great panoramas of the Western Alps, earned with only a few metres of climbing.

sides.character: From La Grave up a tight run of hairpins, a little steeper towards the top, with the Meije behind you and finally before your eyes.
sides.highlights: The Meije from the oratory at the edge of Le Chazelet

plateau-des-glieres.intro: On this plateau above the Thorens valley a Resistance maquis held out in 1944 until it was crushed; the memorial at the top recalls it. The Tour came up in 2018 and 2020, both times with a gravel stretch across the plateau.

sides.character: From Thorens-Glières in steps through forest and meadows, steep ramps alternating with short breathers, and even a brief descent on the way. At the top the plateau opens out all at once.
sides.highlights: The Resistance memorial at the edge of the open plateau.

col-de-sarenne.intro: The Sarenne is the back door of Alpe d'Huez: in the 2013 Tour the race descended it between its two ascents to L'Alpe, much debated at the time for the poor surface. Otherwise hardly anyone comes up here.

sides.character: Short and punchy from Clavans-en-Haut: tight hairpins across open alpine slopes, getting steeper towards the top. No trees, no houses, just the road on the hillside.
sides.highlights: Over the top on into the ski area and down to Alpe d'Huez.

col-du-telegraphe.intro: Hardly anyone rides the Télégraphe for its own sake: it is the first step of the Galibier, and that is how the Tour has known it for decades. It takes its name from the old signal station, and a fort keeps watch above the top.

sides.character: From Saint-Michel-de-Maurienne almost entirely through forest, with the gradient changing more often than the figures suggest. Through the trees, repeated glimpses down into the Maurienne valley.
sides.highlights: From the top you roll down to Valloire, with the Galibier waiting beyond.

valmeinier-1800.intro: A dead end up to the ski station of Valmeinier 1800, meant for anyone staying in Valloire who wants a quiet extra to the Télégraphe and the Galibier. Little known and correspondingly quiet in summer.

sides.character: From the junction in the Valloire basin steadily up through a few hairpins, a little steeper towards the end. A short climb that fits well onto an easy day.

col-du-chaussy.intro: What is famous is not the pass but its base: the Lacets de Montvernier, hairpin upon hairpin stacked into a rock face. Since the Tour discovered them in 2015 they have been among the most photographed stretches of road in the Alps; the Chaussy above remains a quiet mountain road.

sides.character: From Pontamafrey straight into the Montvernier hairpins, then steadily on past hamlets and meadows where the road turns narrow and lonely. A long, even effort with a great many hairpins.
sides.highlights: The view back down from above onto the stacked Montvernier hairpins.

col-du-mollard.intro: The Mollard is the quiet detour from Saint-Jean-de-Maurienne towards the Croix de Fer: long, little used and for long stretches in forest. Those who ride it usually want to spare themselves the traffic of the big passes.

sides.character: Long and in steps: from Saint-Jean-de-Maurienne up through forest and hamlets, with flatter stretches and a short descent along the way. Only at the very top does the country open out.
sides.highlights: At the top the view of the Aiguilles d'Arves.

col-du-pre.intro: The Col du Pré is the hard, beautiful way into the Beaufortain: steeply up through forest, then the Lac de Roselend lies below you. The Tour took it in 2018 before the Cormet de Roselend.

sides.character: From Beaufort via Arêches through many hairpins in shaded forest, the ramps getting steeper rather than easier towards the top. The view only opens at the summit.
sides.highlights: From the top the Lac de Roselend seen from above, with the road to the Cormet beyond.

col-des-aravis.intro: One of the oldest Tour passes, on the programme as early as 1911 and back again and again since. Not a hard climb, but a fine one: meadows, wooden chalets and Mont Blanc facing you at the top.

sides.character: From Flumet via La Giettaz upwards in moderate steps, with flatter stretches between the ramps. Towards the top the valley opens out, green and wide.
sides.highlights: At the top the view of Mont Blanc, and cafés.

col-des-saisies.intro: At the top lies the ski resort of Les Saisies, venue of the Olympic cross-country races in 1992. As a road the pass is wide and well built, the comfortable link between the Beaufortain and the Val d'Arly.

sides.character: From Hauteluce on a wide road, the gradient switching between short steeper ramps and flatter stretches. At the top, broad alpine pastures and the ski resort.
sides.highlights: Down in Hauteluce, the church tower with the Mont Blanc massif behind it.

col-de-la-forclaz-de-montmin.intro: The pass above the Lac d'Annecy where paragliders launch on fine days. From the top the whole lake lies beneath you, which is why, despite its short ascent, it is one of the classics around Annecy.

sides.character: From Talloires moderately at first above the lakeshore, then increasingly steep towards the top, with the last kilometres the hardest. The lake stays behind you almost all the way.
sides.highlights: At the top the view straight down onto the Lac d'Annecy and the launching paragliders.

semnoz.intro: Annecy's home mountain, straight from the lakeshore up to the Crêt de Châtillon. In 2013 the Tour's penultimate stage finished here, won by Nairo Quintana. At the top the panorama reaches from the Bauges to Mont Blanc.

sides.character: From Annecy long and steady through forest, with no real break and no nasty surprises. Only above the tree line does the summit ridge open out.
sides.highlights: On the Crêt de Châtillon the panorama as far as Mont Blanc.

col-de-romme.intro: Since 2009 the Romme has been known as the hard starter before the Colombière when the Tour rides the two back to back. It clings like a balcony above the Arve valley and saves its steepest part for the top.

sides.character: From Cluses gently for a long time, then in steps much steeper on a narrow road above the valley. The average deceives: the upper part is far harder than the lower.
sides.highlights: Views straight down into the Arve valley from the balcony road.

col-de-la-ramaz.intro: A Chablais pass for those seeking quiet: hardly any traffic, a steep middle section around 10 % and a gallery. At the top no ski resort, just alpine pasture.

sides.character: From Taninges in steps: after a moderate start comes the steep middle section with the gallery, then it eases again up to the pasture.

col-d-ornon.intro: The Ornon is the friendly pass of the Oisans: even, open all year and away from the bustle around Alpe d'Huez. It links Le Bourg-d'Oisans with the quiet Valbonnais.

sides.character: From Le Bourg-d'Oisans through the narrow gorge of the Lignarre, then up the valley in gentle steps. Few hairpins, more a long roll uphill.
sides.highlights: On the way the hairpin road to Villard-Reymond branches off.

villard-reymond.intro: A detour for anyone who finds the Ornon too tame: the narrow road winds up in hairpins to a small mountain village high above the Oisans. Hardly any traffic, but plenty of gradient.

sides.character: From the junction on the Ornon road narrow and irregularly steep, hairpin after hairpin up the slope. The gradient changes all the time, and a rhythm is hard to find.
sides.highlights: At the top the view down into the Oisans.

col-du-noyer.intro: The Noyer is the balcony between the Champsaur and the Dévoluy: the road clings to a rock wall, and from the top you look out over the whole Champsaur. Little traffic, and scenically one of the great passes of the southern Western Alps.

sides.character: From Saint-Bonnet easy at first through the meadows of the Champsaur, then steeper in steps, until the final kilometres pull up the wall in hairpins.
sides.highlights: From the top the view across the whole Champsaur.

col-de-montgenevre.intro: One of the oldest crossings of the Alps; the Romans already passed here on their way to Italy. Today it is the main road from Briançon to Turin, open all year, for cyclists more a link than a destination.

sides.character: From Briançon on a wide, well-built road in moderate steps, a few broad hairpins and plenty of traffic. Behind you the fortifications of Briançon fall away.
sides.highlights: The view back to the Vauban fortifications of Briançon.

col-de-braus.intro: In the hinterland of Nice, where the pros train in winter, the Braus is a fixture. It is known for the ladder of hairpins above L'Escarène, laid into the slope like a drawing.

sides.character: From L'Escarène straight into the ladder of hairpins, with the steepest bits early and easier going towards the top. One hairpin follows the next, and the view keeps falling back into the valley.
sides.highlights: From above the view of the hairpin ladder over L'Escarène.

col-de-vence.intro: From Vence up onto a bare karst plateau above the Côte d'Azur, one of the training climbs of the pros around Nice and often part of Paris–Nice too. Short, rideable all year and with the sea at your back.

sides.character: From Vence steadily across open, stony slopes with hardly any shade. The higher you get, the further the view reaches back over the coast.
sides.highlights: The view back over the coast to the sea.

col-de-la-madone.intro: From sea level in Menton to over 900 m: the Madone is the form test of the pros on the Côte d'Azur, where times were compared for years. With only a village at the top, it is almost free of traffic.

sides.character: From Menton moderate at first, then getting steeper towards the top past the perched village of Sainte-Agnès. Many hairpins over dry slopes, the sea always below.
sides.highlights: Near Sainte-Agnès the view down onto Menton and the sea.

col-saint-martin.intro: The pass where the small station of La Colmiane sits links the Vésubie with the Valdeblore. A short, friendly climb in the hinterland of Nice, which the Tour also crossed in 2020.

sides.character: From Saint-Martin-Vésubie steadily through forest, with no surprises and only a few hairpins. Good as a warm-up or as part of a bigger loop.

route-de-presles.intro: One of the bold cliff roads of the Vercors: it hangs above the walls of Choranche and slips through a handful of tunnels. At the top it ends in the village of Presles, with the Bourne far below.

sides.character: Up from Pont-en-Royans, moderate at first, then steeper as the road reaches the cliff and runs through the tunnels. The drop is beside you the whole way.
sides.highlights: The view down over the walls of Choranche into the Bourne valley.

gorges-du-nan.intro: Cut into the wall in 1894 without a parapet, the road through the Gorges du Nan is among the wildest in the Vercors. Three short unlit tunnels, nothing but air below, and hardly any traffic.

sides.character: Up from Cognin-les-Gorges with a changing, at times stiff gradient, until the road hangs in the wall as a narrow ribbon. Up to Malleval, from where it carries on towards the Col du Mont Noir.
sides.highlights: The ledge cut into the rock, without a parapet, high above the Nan.

gorges-du-cians.intro: One of the most impressive gorges of the Maritime Alps: in the upper part red schist almost closes over the road, with narrow tunnels in between. It leads from the Var up to Beuil, the gateway to Valberg.

sides.character: From Touët-sur-Var flat to moderate for a long way through the gorge, with steps and a short descent. Grey rock lower down, red schist higher up, before the final climb to Beuil.
sides.highlights: The narrowest point in the red schist, where the walls almost meet above the road.

gorges-de-daluis.intro: The red canyon of the upper Var, often compared with the Colorado: the road runs on galleries and through tunnels high above the water. Hardly any gradient, but uninterrupted scenery.

sides.character: From Daluis to Guillaumes an up and down with no real net gain, across galleries and through short tunnels. More looking than climbing.
sides.highlights: The Pont de la Mariée high above the gorge.

corniche-sublime.intro: The south side of the Grand Canyon du Verdon: the road follows the rim, and from the Balcons de la Mescla you look some 250 m down onto the confluence of the Verdon and the Artuby. A day with more stops than kilometres.

sides.character: From Aiguines to Comps-sur-Artuby a long up and down along the rim of the gorge, with some hairpins and stiff counter-climbs. Hardly any net height, but a good deal more work than the figure suggests.
sides.highlights: The Balcons de la Mescla and the high bridge over the Artuby.

gorges-de-la-nesque.intro: A balcony road that climbs almost imperceptibly, opposite the rock mass of the Rocher du Cire. The scenic way from the Carpentras side to Sault and so to the foot of the Ventoux.

sides.character: From Villes-sur-Auzon to Sault a long, gentle rise along the gorge wall, with steps and a descent in between. Not a climb for suffering, but one for looking.
sides.highlights: The viewpoint opposite the Rocher du Cire.

gorges-du-guil.intro: The Combe du Queyras is the gateway to the Queyras: a road on galleries and through tunnels above the Guil. Where it emerges from the gorge at the top, the Izoard and the Agnel branch off.

sides.character: From Guillestre up the gorge in gentle steps, with the occasional descent along the way. More a long approach to the big passes than a climb in its own right.
sides.highlights: At the end of the gorge the fort of Château-Queyras on its rock.

sommet-bucher.intro: A lookout summit in the middle of the Queyras, reached by a narrow paved forest road. At the top an all-round view opens over the valleys and mountains of the Queyras.

sides.character: From Ville-Vieille steadily steep through larch forest, hairpin after hairpin on a narrow road. No resting point up to the summit, but a reliable rhythm.
sides.highlights: From the summit, the all-round view over the Guil and Aigue Agnelle valleys.

vallee-de-la-claree.intro: One of the loveliest valleys in the Western Alps: larches, old hamlets and a stream, with the upper part closed to cars on summer days. Little gradient, plenty of scenery, right next to Briançon.

sides.character: From Val-des-Prés up the valley via Névache to Laval, gentle and in steps, a little steeper at the top. The further you go, the quieter and wilder the valley becomes.
sides.highlights: The hamlets of Névache and the quiet head of the valley at Laval.

vallee-de-l-ubaye.intro: The upper Ubaye valley is one of the quietest roads in the Western Alps and ends at Maljasset beneath the three-thousanders. A valley for an easy ride, far from pass traffic.

sides.character: From Saint-Paul-sur-Ubaye up the valley a rolling up and down with short ramps and descents, hardly any net gradient. The valley grows ever narrower and more ringed by high peaks.

fouillouse.intro: A short, steep detour from the upper Ubaye valley to the hamlet of Fouillouse below the Chambeyron massif. On the way the road crosses the Ubaye on a high bridge.

sides.character: From the junction in the Ubaye valley stiff right away and steeper still towards the top, through a few hairpins to the hamlet. Short, but no respite.
sides.highlights: The Pont du Châtelet high above the Ubaye.

vallee-des-chapieux.intro: From Bourg-Saint-Maurice via Les Chapieux into the Vallée des Glaciers, until the road stops at the foot of the Mont Blanc massif. A world's end of pastures and glaciers, away from the Roselend traffic.

sides.character: From Bourg-Saint-Maurice through forest in hairpins at first, then along the valley, sometimes flatter, sometimes steeper, to Les Chapieux and on along a narrow road to the valley head.
sides.highlights: The end of the road in front of the glaciers of the Mont Blanc massif.

cirque-du-fer-a-cheval.intro: A valley head near Sixt, ringed by a semicircle of 700-metre walls with waterfalls pouring down them. Six easy kilometres to one of the great sights of the Northern Alps.

sides.character: From Sixt-Fer-à-Cheval almost flat along the Giffre, a few gentle steps and hardly a bend. The walls draw closer with every kilometre.
sides.highlights: The waterfalls in the semicircle of the valley head.

passo-di-costalunga.intro: The Karerpass is the main road from the Eggental into the Val di Fassa and correspondingly busy. It is worth riding all the same: just below the top the Karersee and the Rosengarten wall lie along the way.

sides.character: From Welschnofen with a changing gradient and a few hairpins through forest, past the Karersee, with the Latemar and the Rosengarten in view. The more varied side, better ridden upwards.
sides.highlights: The Karersee with the Latemar behind it, just below the top.

sides.character: From Vigo di Fassa gentle and in steps on a wide road with hardly any hairpins. More a feeder going up, but a flowing descent into the Val di Fassa.

nigerpass.intro: The quiet side door to the Rosengarten: while through traffic takes the Karerpass, this road climbs steeply and in shade up from Tiers. At the top the wall stands right above you.

sides.character: From Tiers through forest, getting steeper towards the top, with a number of hairpins. Only just below the top do the trees fall back and reveal the Rosengarten wall.
sides.highlights: The Rosengarten wall directly above the top of the pass.

passo-valles.intro: The Valles links the Biois valley with the Travignolo valley and is usually ridden in a loop with the Rolle and San Pellegrino. Narrow and little used, with the Paneveggio forest on the west side and open pastures at the top.

sides.character: From Falcade long and steadily steep, with a few hairpins and the final kilometres above the tree line. The harder side, and one that rewards a good rhythm.
sides.highlights: The open pastures above the tree line before the top.

sides.character: From Paneveggio short, with barely a hairpin, through the forest at first and then steeper to the top. Downhill the calmer line back towards the Rolle.
sides.highlights: The spruce forest of Paneveggio, famous for its tonewood.

monte-bondone.intro: Trento's home mountain and a Giro climb since 1956, the year Charly Gaul won here in a snowstorm. From the Adige it climbs over 1,400 metres in one go, through dozens of hairpins.

sides.character: From Trento off the valley floor, hairpin after hairpin, getting steeper towards the top. Long and hard, the classic Giro ascent with the city and the Adige valley below you.
sides.highlights: Views down onto Trento and the Adige valley.

sides.character: From Sardagna, already well above Trento, steadily steep through many hairpins. Shorter than the main ascent, but without any flat stretches.

passo-tre-croci.intro: The low saddle between Cristallo and Sorapiss links Cortina with Misurina. In the Giro d'Italia it has several times been the approach to the summit finish at the Tre Cime; on its own it is a short, friendly climb through forest.

sides.character: Out of Cortina evenly through larch forest, a few hairpins and a little steeper in the upper part. The pass's real ascent, and the nicer direction to ride it uphill.
